findings.title: The `"numpy"` backend measures Numba, and the registry does not select the compute substrate
findings.description:
The Overview states the harness "ships against the **NumPy** backend (the only backend that exists today)" and the Scopes list puts "Numba backend runner" out of scope. Both are stale. Slice 118 is complete and merged: `src/migratory/engine/_jit_config.py` defines `USE_JIT_KERNELS: bool = True` as the *default*, and the five `BulkForce` classes in `flocking.py`/`herding.py` dispatch to `forces_jit` kernels whenever that flag is true (`CHANGELOG.md`, slice 118 entry; performance journal Entry 9 records 129 TPS on the JIT path vs 103 TPS on the NumPy reference at N=2492).

The design's NumPy runner calls `migratory.engine.tick.tick()` (line 541), which walks the force list and dispatches through that global flag. Nothing in the slice design sets it false or even mentions it. So the JSON report will carry `"backend": "numpy"` over measurements produced by Numba.

This is an architectural boundary problem, not just a label: the design's line 341-343 says slice 144 will register `numba` "that delegates to `engine.forces_jit` via the engine's existing JIT-config flag." That means the harness's two "backends" would be the same `tick()` call with a module-global boolean flipped — the `BackendRunner` registry is a *second* backend-selection mechanism that does not control the substrate it claims to select. That also makes `--list-backends` and `--all-backends` misleading today, and would have two runners contending over one process global once 144 lands (the design's own Open Question about subprocess isolation brushes against this but defers it).

Concrete requirement left unmet: slice plan entry 141 requires timings "across NumPy, Numba, and Quadrants backends" and slice 142 is defined as benchmarking Quadrants "against the existing NumPy and Numba implementations." Neither comparison is possible if "NumPy" *is* Numba. The plan's own condition for deferring the Numba runner — "Numba and Quadrants slot in as those backends become available" — no longer holds for Numba.

Fix before proceeding: (a) state explicitly that the NumPy runner sets `_jit_config.USE_JIT_KERNELS = False` (restoring the verbatim NumPy reference paths the 118 parity tests already exercise), (b) make the substrate choice a per-run runner parameter rather than a process global, and (c) register the already-available Numba runner in this slice, or state in the design why the plan's comparability requirement is now 142's instead.

findings.title: Per-force timing breakdown is deferred, but the slice plan assigns it to this slice
findings.description:
Slice plan entry 141 lists the harness output as "per-tick timings broken down by phase (spatial build, spatial query, CSR assembly, **force totals per force**, integration)." The design states "`force_total` is one number, not per-force, in this slice. Slice 142 introduces per-force timings."

Deferring this is defensible on cost grounds — and the design explains the extension point (`force_breakdown: dict[str, int] | None`) — but it is scope the plan entry explicitly assigns here, and the architecture's "the bottleneck moves" principle is exactly what per-force resolution exists to serve. A single `force_total` cannot answer "which force dominates at which formation," which is the question slice 142's go/no-go gate turns on. Either narrow the `PhaseTimings` gap into this slice, or have the design say plainly that it is amending plan entry 141's stated output and why.

findings.title: No measurement-fidelity NFR, so harness numbers are not anchored to the architecture's stated targets
findings.description:
The architecture states its baseline as "3,500 entities at 57 TPS" and gives a per-phase budget (spatial_build 0.35 ms, spatial_query 5.67 ms, csr_assembly 0.21 ms, force_total 3.14 ms, integrate 0.06 ms). The design restates those numbers (verification step 9) but only as an eyeball shape check: "explicit ms thresholds are not asserted (host variance)." Nowhere does the slice state what its own numbers must agree with, nor the instrumentation's overhead budget — how much `tick_instrumented`'s `perf_counter_ns` bracketing plus its duplicated Python bookkeeping is allowed to inflate a measured tick. Effort is 3/5 and the whole slice exists to produce decision-grade numbers.

The architecture's principle is explicit that "synthetic benchmarks are supplemented with live-server measurements across formation states, since performance is formation-dependent," and the performance journal repeatedly shows synthetic and live diverging (Entry 7: 1.07× synthetic vs 1.05–1.3× live; "single-point benchmarks lie"). With world-server-in-the-loop explicitly out of scope, this harness becomes the sole instrument, so it needs a stated fidelity target (e.g. harness TPS at N=3500 within X% of the live server, or an instrumented-vs-uninstrumented `tick()` delta budget) that later slices can cite when a number is disputed. Without it, slice 142's measured go/no-go has no calibrated reference and "did the change help, by how much" is unanswerable in absolute terms.

findings.title: Named profile/force resolution sources do not exist, and the design invents the profiles it claims not to invent
findings.description:
Line 371: "Profile names resolve against `migratory.engine.profile` presets." Line 393-395: "Force names resolve to module-level singleton instances in the relevant engine modules (e.g. `flocking.cohesion_force`)." Neither exists. `src/migratory/engine/profile.py` defines the `BehavioralProfile` type, not a named preset registry; `flocking.py`/`herding.py` define force *classes* and no module-level singleton instances (grep for `cohesion_force` / `name_force =` returns nothing).

Compounding this, line 392-396 asserts "The harness does not invent new profiles." But `config/default.yaml` defines exactly one profile, `"default"`; the design's `flocker`/`leader` mix (95%/5%, `leadership_weight: 0.2`) has no counterpart there. So the harness establishes its own operating point while the `mid-flock.yaml` comment claims it is "roughly equivalent to the live-server default config formation state at steady state" — which is also not true of `config/default.yaml` (100 agents, 20 TPS, 1000×1000 world). The upshot is a hidden dependency: cross-backend parity comparisons in 142/145 will be made against a hand-built profile mix that no server config exercises, so a parity failure cannot be attributed to the substrate rather than the harness's own setup. The design should name the real source (`BehavioralProfile` constructed in the harness from workload fields), state that these are harness-local reference profiles, and drop "resolve against presets" / "module-level singletons."

findings.title: `tick_instrumented` is a full parallel copy of the tick body, and the stated mitigation cannot detect the failure mode it names
findings.description:
The Risk section names drift between `tick_instrumented()` and `tick()` as the top technical risk, admits that "drift in the *phase boundaries* (the timings become misleading without changing correctness) is not detectable mechanically," and offers as mitigation a test asserting bit-equal `TickResult` output. That test cannot cover the admitted failure mode: bit-equal positions are exactly what a wrong phase bracket still produces.

The design also undersells the cost. Instrumenting the five phases means reproducing the entire tick body — spatial build, the `all_capped` fast-path branch, the general path with `apply_neighbor_cap`, `exclude_self`, `offsets`/`cumsum` CSR assembly, the force loop, profile-attribute fancy indexing, and `integrate` — roughly a 110-line function carried in `bench/backends/numpy_backend.py`, against `CLAUDE.md`'s "do not duplicate logic" and ~300-line file guidance. The document describes it as "~5 lines per phase," which reads as an understatement that hides the real maintenance surface.

This is the one place where the *heavier* option may be the cheaper one: the deferred `tick(..., profiler=...)` parameter cost one `if profiler:` branch per phase in the engine and would make boundary drift structurally impossible. The design rejects it on the grounds that the engine "is a clean room" and slice 140's contract is preserved — a legitimate concern — but the document should either accept the full duplication size explicitly (and say why the `profiler` hook is still the wrong trade), or adopt the hook and give the readers the single source of truth.

findings.title: Failure modes are enumerated for the registry but not for the I/O paths this slice adds, and a stalled run cannot be detected by an automated consumer
findings.description:
The four listed failure modes cover workload-field validation, unregistered backend, `setup()` raising, and TPS < 1. The slice also opens three new I/O paths with no stated behavior: reading workload YAML (missing/unreadable file, malformed YAML, directory given), writing reports (`bench/results/` absent, unwritable, disk full, non-atomic write leaving a truncated JSON that a later comparison tool would parse as valid), and invoking `git rev-parse HEAD` (git absent from PATH, not a repo, detached/being-rewritten). Per project policy ("fail explicitly with errors or obviously-placeholder values"), each needs a named outcome rather than an implicit one.

More substantively, the TPS < 1 case "emits a warning to stderr but writes the report," and the CLI section says exit code is non-zero only "on workload load failure or backend error." A backend that hangs or degrades to 0.5 TPS therefore runs the full 600 measure ticks, writes a syntactically perfect report, and exits 0. There is no wall-clock bound or per-tick timeout on the measure loop. Slice plan entry 141 justifies the harness partly because "per-tier validation can be automated"; with this exit-code contract, an automated per-tier run cannot distinguish a healthy 59 TPS from a stalled one, and will happily record a regression as data. Recommend: a named non-zero exit for the low-TPS/stalled case, and a bound on total run time with an explicit abort message.

findings.title: The `finalize()` teardown hook is an abstraction with no consumer in this slice or its declared interfaces
findings.description:
`BackendRunner.finalize()` is required by the Protocol and invoked in a `try/finally`, but the only registered backend's implementation is a no-op, and the design's own text says so: "a teardown hook (release GPU memory, clean up Numba caches), no-op on NumPy." Its two named justifications are Quadrants device handles (slice 145) and Numba caches — and for Numba, the existing `_warm_force_kernels()` server-startup path and the on-disk cache mean there is nothing to release. This is abstraction a future backend may want but nothing uses yet, and it is the kind of speculative surface the architecture's incremental-migration goal does not require. Cut it from the Protocol and let slice 144/145 add it when a backend actually owns a resource to release; the same goes for the `--list-backends` / `--list-workloads` convenience flags if they are not needed to satisfy any success criterion.

The rest of the design's surface is proportionate: the three-workload set matches the architecture's named formation regimes, the JSON/Markdown pair matches the plan's "machine-readable … plus a human-readable summary," and the registry — unlike `finalize` — is genuinely needed by 142/144/145 and explicitly called for by the plan.

findings.title: `platform.processor()` is not a usable cross-platform comparison key
findings.description: The result header is built from `platform.system()`, `platform.machine()`, `platform.processor()`. `processor()` is empty on many Linux systems — including NVIDIA hosts — and historically reports `i386` on Apple Silicon builds. Since the plan's stated purpose is comparable timings "on Apple Silicon (Metal) and NVIDIA (CUDA)," the metadata that makes two runs comparable should not contain a field that is blank or wrong on the platform Tier 3 depends on. Use `platform.machine()` plus an explicit CPU/GPU device name from the backend, and drop `processor()`.

findings.title: Scope boundaries, dependency direction, and the harness's role as empirical gate match the architecture
findings.description: The out-of-scope list is unusually disciplined and each exclusion is defensible against the architecture: the wire protocol is kept out on the strength of "the wire is a separable problem"; memory measurement is deferred on the strength of the architecture's own conclusion that "memory is not a constraint that gates the roadmap"; the `pytest-benchmark` contract checks from slice 140 are explicitly kept side-by-side rather than replaced; and the harness is correctly positioned as the instrument slices 142–145 read from, with `TickResult` (slice 140) as the only engine boundary crossed. `dependencies: [140-tick-return-type-contract]` matches plan entry 141's "Dependencies: (140)" exactly, and the layering is correct: `bench/` sits above `migratory.engine` and reaches into `migratory_server` nowhere, which is what the architecture's "clean ownership boundaries" goal requires of a compute-side instrument. The GPU-determinism caveat (record the hash, let a downstream consumer apply the tolerance band) is consistent with the architecture's open question on reduction-order non-determinism rather than inventing a threshold here.

Named profile/force resolution sources do not exist, and the design invents the profiles it claims not to invent
`tick_instrumented` is a full parallel copy of the tick body, and the stated mitigation cannot detect the failure mode it names
Failure modes are enumerated for the registry but not for the I/O paths this slice adds, and a stalled run cannot be detected by an automated consumer
The `finalize()` teardown hook is an abstraction with no consumer in this slice or its declared interfaces
`platform.processor()` is not a usable cross-platform comparison key
Scope boundaries, dependency direction, and the harness's role as empirical gate match the architecture
